body:
As we open Parshas Bereishis, we aren’t simply reading about the beginning of the world, we are experiencing a renewal of reality itself. But we do so as people who have just emerged from the intense spiritual journey of Tishrei. We’ve crowned Hashem as King on Rosh Hashanah, purified ourselves on Yom Kippur, and basked in closeness and joy through Sukkos and Simchas Torah.

So what now? How do we carry that spiritual energy forward into the year?

The answer lies not only in the newness of the world, but in the role we play in that renewed world.

From Surrender to Strength

In Sefer Devarim, we saw the continuing theme of bitul, of nullification of my animalistic will before the will of Hashem, and of an individual learning how they are needed and able to contribute to the whole and the greater good.

But before we can surrender to the will of Hashem, we must first believe in the value of the self. Otherwise, what is it that we are surrendering? As we restart the Torah with Parshas Bereishis, a shift occurs. We are reintroduced to ourselves not as just parts of a whole, but as active partners in creation, each and every one of us having this focus and ability.

Hashem says, "נַעֲשֶׂה אָדָם בְּצַלְמֵנוּ" — "Let us make man in Our image" (Bereishis 1:26). Rashi, quoting the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 8:7), explains that Hashem consulted His heavenly court. The act of creation was not unilateral. It was collaborative on one level, but not in essence — because when the Torah describes the actual creation of Adam, it says:

"וַיִּבְרָא א-לֹהִים אֶת הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ" — "And G-d created man in His image" (Bereishis 1:27).

Not in their image. Not in the image of the angels. In Hashem’s image.

And that’s the key: we are not mishutafim because we were created by consensus, we are mishutafim because we were created in His image. And His ratzon, as proven by our very existence, is to create.

That tzelem Elokim is what empowers us to create, to choose, to speak, to shape, and to elevate. It’s not an invitation to arrogance, but a call to responsibility.

The Koach of Speech

The most striking way that man reflects the Divine is in the power of speech. Hashem creates the world through speech. "וַיֹּאמֶר א-לֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר" — "And G-d said: Let there be light" (Bereishis 1:3).

Adam too is granted the power of words. He names each creature in Gan Eden, not arbitrarily, but with insight. The name he gives reflects the inner reality of that being.

But that power can be distorted. When Chava is persuaded by the nachash (snake) to eat from the Eitz HaDaas, she alters Hashem’s words ever so slightly. And Adam, instead of taking responsibility, uses his words to shift blame: “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me from the tree.” Chava then deflects as well: “The serpent deceived me.”

From the beginning, we see the immense weight that words carry. They can name and words can create. But they can also mislead and avoid. The power of creation is in our mouths, but it comes with responsibility.

Had Adam used his power of speech to do Viduy, confession, when Hashem asked him where he was and what he had done, perhaps Hashem would have accepted this teshuva and would have never sent Adam and Chava out of eden to begin with as we are taught that teshuva existed before the world was created.

Created for Me, but Not First

The Gemara in Sanhedrin (37a) teaches that each person must say: “בשבילי נברא העולם” — "The world was created for me."

The human being was created last, not because he is least important, but because he is the purpose of creation.

Yet the very next page (Sanhedrin 38a) offers a critical counterbalance. The Rabbanim in the Gemara teach:

שֶׁאִם תָּזוּחַ דַּעְתּוֹ עָלָיו — אוֹמְרִים לוֹ: יַתּוּשׁ קְדָמְךָ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה בְּרֵאשִׁית — "If he becomes haughty, he is told: The mosquito preceded you in creation."

We are at once the center of the banquet and the last guest to arrive. The universe was prepared for us, but we must enter with humility.

This duality is not a contradiction — it is the posture of a Jew. To carry greatness without arrogance. To bear responsibility without self-importance.

The Moon and Its Message

This balance finds profound expression in the story of the moon.

Rashi (Bereishis 1:16) brings the Midrash (Chullin 60b, Bereishis Rabbah 6:3): at first, the sun and moon were equal. But the moon protested: "Two kings cannot wear one crown." Hashem responded: "Go and diminish yourself."

The moon was made smaller, its light reflective rather than original.

But Hashem consoled the moon. The Jewish people would be linked to it. They would count their months by its phases. Righteous people would be compared to it.

The moon’s power is not in its brightness, but in its timing, its cycles, and its constancy. It pulls the tides, influences the core of the earth, and governs the rhythm of time itself. And yet, it does so humbly, in the background, through borrowed light.

The Jewish people are like the moon. Sometimes full, sometimes diminished. Sometimes celebrated, sometimes forgotten. But we are always necessary. Our presence, even when unseen, sustains the world.

Our Power of Being Creators Through Speech

On Rosh Hashanah, we say “יְהִי רָצוֹן” — “May it be Your will…” We ask for health, for victory, for blessing — not through might or wealth, but through words.

And it is not only with Hashem that our words matter. It is with one another.

A soldier I know told me a story. Over a year ago, he met the father of one of the hostages who has now, baruch Hashem, been released. At the time, the situation seemed hopeless. But this young soldier, just a regular Jew, looked the father in the eye and blessed him, “You will see your son again. Hashem will help you.”

He didn’t know why he said it. He didn’t even fully believe it himself. But he said it out of love, out of care, out of hope. And this week, he saw that father reunited with his son, holding a lulav, embracing in joy.

That is an example of the koach of dibur, the creating power of a Jew’s words. When used properly, we have the ability to comfort, to bless and to impact the world and to even change creation itself.

There was no logical reason to believe that that father would ever be reunited with his son. But through loving compassion, that chayal’s words may have been what was needed to power and to create a newer reality which allowed for that amazing and miraculous reunion.

A Final Charge

The world today feels uncertain. We have experienced loss, fear, and confusion. But the Torah tells us: you matter. You were created for a reason. Your words, your presence, your actions all have the power of creation from Hashem and they can change things.

So as we started with in the beginning, and to remind ourselves again: before we can fully surrender to the will of Hashem, we must first believe in the value of the self, my ability to grant comfort, to change the world, to heal others, and to create.

Parshas Bereishis is a time of renewal. A time to take on new commitments. To set goals. To speak words of love and blessing. To build, not destroy. To reflect light, even if it is borrowed light, for that too is divine.

May we merit to rise and shine again, until the time of Mashiach, when the moon and the sun will once again shine with equal strength, and the light of every Jew will be seen in its full glory.

Shabbat Shalom.

Parshas Noach – A Deeper Look at Tafkid, Messaging, and Identity

This week’s challenge wasn’t in finding Torah to speak about—quite the opposite. There was too much to say. So many ideas, but the delivery felt stuck. And maybe that’s exactly the point: the how of the message depends deeply on the who that is delivering it. Every message must come through the prism of the self. And that’s why this parsha strikes such a chord.

Noach’s Individual Tafkid Noach is called a tzaddik in his generation (Bereishis 6:9). He walked with Hashem. That’s not a side note—it’s a profound identity. But he didn’t do outreach like Avraham. He built the teivah, saved his family, and followed Hashem’s word precisely (Rashi ad loc). That was his avodah. We often focus on what he didn’t do—but what he did do requires enormous strength.

Noach lived in a time of total corruption (Bereishis 6:11). The world had become immoral to the point that even the animals had been influenced (Rashi, Bereishis 6:12). In such a time, Noach’s righteousness was not a passive quality. It was built through boundaries. He created space between himself and the outside. He didn’t absorb the world; he protected his teivah. He may not have brought others in, but he preserved what mattered.

And when people asked him what he was building, he told them and he told them why. He wasn’t silent, he didn’t compromise, and he didn’t lower the message (Sanhedrin 108b). He just didn't go out to tell people the message—he told it to them when they came to him.

The Animal World and Its Reflections Even within the teivah, the avodah was demanding. Noach cared for the animals, but even there, it wasn’t smooth. One time he was late feeding the lion, and the lion bit him (Sanhedrin 108b). We see that even the act of kindness, of duty, can carry risk. Lions are powerful, social animals. Whether it was just a reminder bite or a reflection of a group pack animal on someone who was quiet, there is a lot to learn even from this.

Then, when it came time to re-engage the world, Noach sent out the raven first (Bereishis 8:7). The raven didn’t fulfill the mission. Rashi explains that the raven circled, suspicious that Noach had ulterior motives (Rashi, Bereishis 8:7). But the Gemara in Pesachim 113b hints to us something else: that ravens are among those species that love their own kind.

This is striking. The raven may not have succeeded in this task, but it is a creature of connection and loyalty. Its failure may not be due to selfishness, but rather to a kind of insularity. The raven operates in community. But community alone isn’t always sufficient—sometimes it may only respond to a community.

Later, ravens find their moment. In the days of Eliyahu HaNavi, it is the raven that feeds him (Melachim I 17:4–6). It brings food to the prophet who was in hiding, rejected by society, preserving truth from within. The raven didn't help Noach, but it helped Eliyahu. In the right context, its koach became invaluable.

The Dove and Its Simplicity The dove, on the other hand, fulfills its task (Bereishis 8:11). It flies out, returns with the olive branch. Doves are quiet, personal birds. They don’t nest communally. They aren’t loud. They live simple lives.

And later, we see doves brought as korbanos—for the poor, the recovering mother, the baal teshuva (Vayikra 1:14, 12:8, 14:22). They are korbanos of individuals. Not for the tzibbur. Not for grandeur. The dove speaks to the person who needs something gentle, private, restorative.

In a sense, the raven and the dove represent two modes of mission. The raven, bound by group loyalty, couldn’t reach outward at first. But later, its communal koach served a navi. The dove, by contrast, represents the private healing of the individual.

And here lies a subtle but profound contrast: the raven was not able to respond to the internal, individualized tzaddik like Noach. It needed the external navi—Eliyahu—or perhaps someone like Avraham, to fulfill its purpose. The raven’s strength is communal, activated best in service of those who operate outwards.

But the dove—precisely because of its quiet, personal nature—could respond to Noach. It understood the language of inner worlds. The dove was able to return to the teivah because Noach’s avodah matched its essence: inward, simple, steady.

In this contrast we learn something about ourselves too. Some missions respond only to the one who goes out. Others awaken when met by stillness and depth within. And each is holy in its time.

From Noach to Avraham: A Generational Shift After the mabul, the world rebuilds. But then we see the Tower of Bavel, a massive collective project, but one without proper spiritual grounding (Bereishis 11:4). Mass cooperation aimed in the wrong direction. That’s the shadow side of unity without purpose.

At this point, Avram arises. He is not yet Avraham Avinu, but he already begins to step out. His koach is outreach. He teaches. He spreads the name of Hashem (Bereishis 12:5; Rashi). This is a different tafkid than Noach’s—and it is needed now. And yet, we should note: Noach and Avram overlapped for 57 years (Seder Olam Rabbah ch. 1). The transition was not immediate. Both roles coexisted.

Sometimes the world needs a Noach. Sometimes an Avram. And sometimes both.

How do we prepare ourselves for the world and the water? The mabul water was boiling and acidic, Chazal say it was laced with destructive forces (Rashi, Bereishis 7:23; Sanhedrin 108b). But we also say ein mayim ela Torah (Bava Kamma 17a). Water can destroy, or it can nurture. The same substance, depending on direction.

In the Kuzari (Maamar 3), the Chaver explains that each Jew is like a limb in the body. When connected, the body thrives. When disconnected, the limb is lost. This is true in tefillah, in learning, in communal mission. When we unite b’derech tov, the waters are redemptive.

Mar Cheshvan and the Ten-Day Window The Mabul began on the 17th of Mar Cheshvan (Rashi, Bereishis 7:11). In Eretz Yisrael, we begin davening for rain on the 7th, ten days earlier.

An opportunity to of ten days of preparation, of bracha-seeking before the memory of destruction. Ten days, like Aseres Yemei Teshuva. Like the Ten Utterances. Like the Ten Middos of Hashem.

We are reminded: water is coming. Will it be a mabul or a mikvah?

Sitting at the Feet of Tzaddikim There’s a powerful model that runs through this entire parsha: sitting at the feet of tzaddikim. Chazal teach us to "be covered in the dust of their feet" (Avos 1:4)—to draw near to those who walk the path of truth, even if their styles differ. Noach, Avraham, Yitzchak, Yaakov—each one had a different expression of greatness. And each of them offers something for us. We don’t have to become them, but we can draw from them. Learn from their kochos. Reflect their light. Sometimes we learn to set boundaries; sometimes to tear them down. Sometimes to hold firm; sometimes to reach outward. We don’t follow blindly—we learn with discernment. And through that, we grow.

Final Reflections We are not Noach. We are not Avraham. But we carry something from both. There are times we need to retreat and preserve. There are times we need to step out and speak. The key is to discern which tafkid is ours today. And to never forget that even within what looks like inaction, there may be deep avodah taking place.

May we be zocheh to recognize our individual tafkid, to honor the different voices within our mesorah, and to draw down water that heals and nourishes, not water that floods and burns.

Gut Shabbos.

Lech Lecha: The Beginnings of Z'chut Avot

A Turning Point in Torah

This week’s parsha marks a turning point in the Torah’s story. Until now, Bereishis has been about humanity. With Lech Lecha, Hashem turns His attention to one man, and through Avram, the story of the Avos begins which eventually leads to us.

The Meaning of Z’chus Avos

We often speak about z’chus Avos, the merit of our forefathers, as if it is something automatically inherited, a spiritual trust fund that protects us through life. But z’chus Avos is not just an unearned reward. It is a connection. It means we have access to the same inner strength, the same faith, the same courage that they lived by. To benefit from their z’chus, we must also continue their path. But also, to continue their path, we need to understand what they did which applies to us which can help us access the z'chus.

Before Lech Lecha: The Fire of Faith

To understand who Avram truly was, we must step back to the end of Parshas Noach. That’s where the Midrash first introduces him - a young man who destroyed his father’s idols, who challenged the world’s beliefs, who was thrown into Nimrod’s fiery furnace and emerged alive. Even before Hashem spoke to him directly, Avram was already living a life of faith. He didn’t wait to be chosen; he chose Hashem first.

The Command to Go

When Hashem finally tells him, Lech lecha mei’artzecha - leave your land, your birthplace, your father’s house, Avram had already left Ur Kasdim and was in Charan. So why tell him to go again? Chazal explain that this was not about distance, but about depth. The first journey was physical; the second was spiritual. “Go for yourself,” says Hashem, not to escape the past, but to uncover your essence. Growth is never just about leaving; it is about becoming.

From that moment, Avram’s life becomes a series of journeys, each one testing his faith and refining his soul. He leaves behind familiarity and comfort. He faces famine and descends to Egypt. He risks his life to rescue Lot. Each time, he moves forward, not backward. Each time, he discovers a new dimension of emunah - a faith that does not depend on comfort or certainty.

The Fear in Egypt - Seeing the Best in Others

One puzzling moment stands out: when Avram tells Sarai, “Please say you’re my sister.” How could the man who survived being put into a fiery furnace fear for his life? The mefarshim explain that Avram did not doubt Hashem’s power, he doubted his worthiness. Perhaps he thought he had already used up his miracles. And yet, even in fear, he acted with faith, protecting his wife and trusting Hashem to do what was right.

There is a deeper beauty here. The Midrash says that just as Avram trusted that Sarai would be saved through her own righteousness, Sarai trusted that Avram would be saved through his. Each believed in the other more than in themselves. Avram and Sarai lived that balance. They looked outward with love and inward with honesty. The Lubavitcher Rebbe taught that people will often look at others with the right eye, with kindness and generosity, and at themselves with the left eye, with stringency, which may have been what Avram and Sarai at that point in time were doing. But a way that we can heal over time as well is to learn to look at ourselves and others with both eyes in a fair and balanced way which we can see as they both see their own value more and more throught the coming parshiot.

The Courage to Risk for Others

Later, when Avram fought the war of the kings to rescue Lot, we see his truer colors start to come out as he risks himself for others, guided not by self-interest but by conscience. That is Lech Lecha in its purest form, to go to yourself, to go beyond yourself, and to go for yourself. It is a journey of constant growth, of never being satisfied with who we were yesterday.

Beyond the Stars

Life brings us tests. It asks us to step into the unknown, to leave behind what feels safe. But that’s precisely where growth happens. When Hashem took Avram “outside,” showing him the stars and saying, “Look toward the heavens… so shall your children be,” He was teaching him that faith itself must rise above nature. Avram could not have children according to the stars, so Hashem lifted him beyond them. He didn’t just change Avram’s fate; He changed the very definition of faith.

The Midrashim say and the Mepharshim explain that Hashem took Avram out of this world and past the stars that exist. He said that just because you are right now Avram and your wife is Sarai doesn't mean that you will always have to be that way. Avram had the courage to follow through with his emunah in Hashem and His promises, to change himself so that he would be continuously going out to himself and out to others together. This is the lesson we bring from Avram Avinu, not even from Avraham, but from Avram. In our earliest stages, we can already start to change who we are, what our reality is, what our direction and purpose are. And then as we, their legacy, live forward this way, we get to tap into z’chus avos.

Personal Reflection

My own life, in its own humble way, echoes a lot of this message. I grew up in California, far from the life I live today. Through challenges, moves, and changes, I found myself learning Torah in Baltimore, and ultimately, Baruch Hashem, here in Eretz Yisrael. Each transition came with uncertainty, often not generated by want but rather a push from something bigger and greater than myself, but also with the quiet voice of Lech Lecha. Move forward, keep growing, trust the process. Looking back, I can see how each step, even the difficult ones, was guided by Hashem’s hand and has helped me to develop who I am today, someone who, like Avraham Avinue, went out not just to himself but for others as well.

Our Living Legacy

Avram and Sarai began as a couple who could not have children. Yet today, we - their descendants - are the proof of what faith can create. We are their living legacy, the continuation of that moment when Hashem said, “Look up.”

The Call of Lech Lecha

As we enter Shabbos Lech Lecha, we can all hear that same call: Lech lecha - go forward. Step out of what’s familiar. Not because we’re unworthy, but because we are worthy of growing further. Like Avram, we too are invited to move beyond the limits of nature, beyond the stories we tell ourselves, and to walk toward the person Hashem knows we can become.

A Few Questions for Self-Reflection

● How am I going out of myself to grow?

● Am I standing up for what is right?

● Am I looking at myself and others in a way of dan l’zchus?

Parshas Vayeira – The Rule of Three

Introduction: The Power of Three

Parshas Vayeira is one of those unmistakably powerful parshiyos, undeniably rich, emotionally resonant, and full of transformative lessons. Since Torah is hora’ah,a guide for living,this parsha offers a unique chance to learn and grow in the moment.

As we transition from last week's parsha to this one, and look forward to the next, we walk in the footsteps of Avraham Avinu. A fascinating pattern arises,a "rule of three" that surfaces not just here, but across Torah. More often than not, when we encounter a group of three, it's for the good.

This week, we see the three malachim who visit Avraham; the three se’ah of flour that Sarah prepares; and the three-year-old animals brought at the Bris Bein HaBesarim, where there are three types of animals (a cow, a goat, and a ram), three of each, plus additional birds,a pattern of threes within threes. In other cases, we find offerings of three one-year-old animals.

Even in our Shabbos tefillos, we see a triple expression,"ba, bo, bam",appearing in the section about the sanctity of the day, linked to Shacharis, Mincha, and Ma’ariv.

Clearly, three is not just a number. It’s a rhythm, a framework, a sacred pattern.

The Unique Three: Akeidas Yitzchak

But one “three” in this parsha stands apart.

When Hashem tells Avraham to bring his son to the Akeidah, the command includes a trio of emotionally charged terms:

“Take now your son, your only one, the one you love,Yitzchak.” "קח נא את בנך את יחידך אשר אהבת את יצחק" (בראשית כב:ב)

This pasuk is so foundational, it appears in our daily tefillos.

Rashi explains that Hashem was speaking with kindness, gently preparing Avraham for the unimaginable: offering his own son, the one through whom the entire Jewish future was meant to unfold.

But the Sfas Emes opens a deeper perspective: Each of these phrases represents another level of mesirus nefesh,self-sacrifice.

● Bincha – Your son. A basic connection. Possibly one of many.

● Yechidcha – Your only one. Singular, exclusive, irreplaceable.

● Asher ahavta – The one you love. An emotional, deeply personal bond.

Each phrase ascends in intensity. Each step raises the cost,and the spiritual reward,of sacrifice.

What’s the Message for Us?

Had Hashem said simply, “Take Yitzchak,” Avraham would have complied without question. He lived as a merkavah, a pure vehicle of the Divine Will.

So why include so many extra words?

Because Torah teaches for eternity. The Midrashim and Mefarshim reveal that this wasn’t only for Avraham,it was for us. For future generations who would need to develop their own capacities for giving, for sacrifice, for climbing spiritual levels.

Sometimes we give up something minor. Sometimes it’s significant. Sometimes it’s something we deeply love. That’s the process of spiritual growth.

Mesirus Nefesh and the Three Cardinal Sins

This triad also mirrors the three cardinal sins,the aveiros for which a Jew must give up their life rather than transgress:

● Avodah Zarah – Idolatry

● Giluy Arayos – Forbidden sexual relationships

● Shefichas Damim – Murder

The source for this is found in Gemara Sanhedrin 74a:

"Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: From where do we know that one must give up their life rather than commit idolatry, forbidden relations, or murder? Because it says: ‘And you shall love Hashem your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your might’ (Devarim 6:5),even if He takes your soul."

אמר רב יהודה אמר רב: מנין לעבודה זרה וגילוי עריות ושפיכות דמים שייהרג ואל יעבור? שנאמר: "ואהבת את ה' אלקיך בכל לבבך ובכל נפשך ובכל מאדך" (דברים ו:ה) – אפילו נוטל את נפשך.

Now, look again at the three phrases:

● Bincha – A child. In holiness, a child is the result of a mitzvah. But from giluy arayos, the result is distorted. According to some opinions, a mamzer’s atonement only comes through generational suffering or fire at the end of days.

● Yechidcha – The only one. The concept of “only one” links to the Oneness of Hashem. Idolatry is its opposite. Letting go of our personal "yechid" for Hashem is a form of devotion that counteracts Avodah Zarah.

● Asher ahavta – Love. Love can inspire the highest good or lead to the worst crimes of passion. Torah love uplifts. Unchecked love can lead to jealousy and, tragically, murder.

Each phrase aligns with one sin,and each also offers its tikkun. Through Avraham’s layered mesirus nefesh, we learn how to cleanse, uplift, and live with purpose.

A Pattern That Extends Throughout Torah

Avraham didn’t just pass a test. He mapped a blueprint for generations.

This pattern of three continues:

● The Akeidah occurred on the third day.

● We celebrate Shalosh Regalim.

● We descend from the three Avos: Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov.

● Even the word Av (father) equals three in gematria.

When a father acts with righteousness and love, and the children reflect that back, a third entity emerges, the Shechinah, resting between them. It's a Divine triangle.

Closing Reflection

Our Avos gave us a gift: a way to live with spiritual awareness, personal integrity, and deep connection to Hashem. It’s our turn to take that gift seriously.

So I stop and ask myself:

● What have I given up out of love for Hashem?

● What have I surrendered that is uniquely mine?

● What small comforts or habits have I sacrificed for a higher purpose?

And most importantly: What is it within me, what spark of inherent worth, what inner strength or soul-rooted depth, makes me even capable of offering things up for Hashem and those around me? What gives me the merit to be counted among those who live a life of such avodah? Where does that quiet, sacred courage come from, and how do I continue to honor it?

Because I love my Av, And I love Hashem.

Have a wonderful, wonderful Shabbos.

D'var Torah: Parshat Chayei Sarah

The Power of the Imahot: Nature, Nurture, and Rising Above

Introduction: It's Not Just About the Fathers

In the last several weeks, we've been talking about zechut Avot, the power and impact of the fathers. But truth be told, it's not just all about the fathers. As we discussed in last week's parsha when we looked at the concept of three, it's a husband, a wife, and Hashem together that make a child and bring this world into focus. The partnership of these three brings blessing, continuity, and purpose to the world.

As we refocus on this week's parsha, Chayei Sarah, we see zechut Imahot, the power and the zechut that we gain from the mothers. Their influence reverberates not only through our history, but in every Jewish home and every Jewish heart. Another concept we see in this week's parsha, and in future parshiot as well, is a deeper understanding of something that goes back and forth in our world today: the concept of nature versus nurture.

Chayei Sarah: A Life of Completion

At the very beginning of the parsha, we encounter remarkable words:

"And the life of Sarah was one hundred years and twenty years and seven years; the years of Sarah's life." ויהיו חיי שרה מאה שנה ועשרים שנה ושבע שנים שני חיי שרה (Bereishit 23:1)

The way the verse is structured is unusual. Rashi explains that the Torah breaks down Sarah's age into separate segments to teach us something profound: at a hundred she was as free of sin as at twenty (when one reaches the age of responsibility), and at twenty she was as beautiful as at seven. She lived a complete life, a life of shleimut. The repetition of "the years of Sarah's life" teaches us that all her years were equally good.

The Midrash Tanchuma (Vayeira 23) relates that among the factors that brought about Sarah's death was news of the Akeidah. The Satan came to Sarah disguised as Yitzchak and told her that Avraham had taken him to a mountain, built an altar, arranged wood, bound him, and was about to slaughter him when Hashem's angel intervened. Upon hearing this, Sarah's soul departed from her.

But I want to offer a different perspective here, one rooted in Chassidic teachings. There's a profound teaching brought down by the Baal Shem Tov and other teachers: when a person completes their tafkid in this world, when they've fulfilled the specific mitzvah for which they were created, their soul may return to its Source if it no longer needs to remain in this world.

This concept goes back to being shutaf with Hashem, that we are partners with Him in creation. That's our side of the partnership: creating that which He needs us to create in this world. Not to say He couldn't do it on His own, but this is the design, the goal, the way He built us and built the world.

Sarah's tafkid, her mission, was Yitzchak. Not just to give birth to him, but to ensure he was brought up in such a way that he himself would have the strength and spiritual preparation to fulfill his role in the Akeidah. Consider this: he was 37 years old when the Akedat Yitzchak happened. A 37 year old intelligent man is not going to arbitrarily lie down on a sacrificial altar with his father holding a knife over him. Something profound was infused in him by both parents to bring about his ability to follow through with this. That chinuch, that spiritual education, came in large part from his mother, Sarah.

Once Sarah's mission was fulfilled, once she had raised Yitzchak to this level of faith and commitment, her neshamah had completed its work in this world. At this stage, we can understand her passing not as tragedy alone, but as the natural completion of a life lived with perfect shleimut.

The Mother's Role in Chinuch: The Foundation of Jewish Education

The foundation of Jewish chinuch comes from the mother. This is explicit in our tradition. The Midrash in Shemot Rabbah (28:2) discusses why Hashem instructed Moshe to speak first to the women when giving the Torah, explaining: "Why were the women first? Because they are zealous in mitzvot. Alternatively, so that they could teach their children Torah."

The mother's sacred role includes teaching the children the Shema. The very first learning of the Shema typically comes from the mother. Think about what the Shema represents: it is the ability to say, "I am nothing without Hashem." It's an ultimate statement of bittul, of nullifying oneself before the Creator. This is the deepest foundation a mother can give, teaching a child from the earliest age that we exist in partnership with Hashem, that everything we have and everything we are comes from Him.

We can see the impact, the tafkid, the sacred work of mothers coming to fruition through generations. This is not just about biological motherhood, but about the spiritual role that Jewish women play in ensuring the continuity of our people and our Torah.

Rivka: The Return of Sarah's Miracles

The parsha continues with a beautiful transition. When Rivka came from her home and was brought by Yitzchak to Sarah's tent, something extraordinary happened. Rashi (Bereishit 24:67) explains that when Rivka entered that sacred space, the miracles that had characterized Sarah's tent during her lifetime returned.

What were these miracles? The Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 60:16) teaches that three miraculous signs accompanied Sarah's righteousness. First, the Shabbat candles she lit would burn from one Shabbat eve to the next Shabbat eve. Second, there was a blessing in her dough that ensured it never spoiled. Third, a cloud of glory hovered over her tent, a sign of the Divine Presence dwelling there.

These three miracles correspond to the three primary mitzvot associated with Jewish women: lighting Shabbat candles (ner), separating challah (challah), and maintaining family purity (niddah). Through these mitzvot, a Jewish woman creates a dwelling place for the Shechinah, bringing Hashem's presence into the home in a tangible way.

The teaching also tells us that a husband cannot be fully connected to his wife while his mother is still present in the same way. This is not to suggest a mother's influence is negative, but rather to acknowledge that a mother's presence continues to shape her son's life even after he marries. There comes a time when a man must fully cleave to his wife and establish an independent household. Only when Rivka fully stepped into Sarah's role could Yitzchak be comforted for the loss of his mother, because he saw that the legacy would continue.

Nature versus Nurture: Breaking the Mold

These concepts go hand in hand with understanding how we grow beyond our circumstances. Let's step back and trace this theme through our forefathers.

Adam HaRishon had no one to nurture him, only the nature that Hashem created within him. Yet even that pure nature, combined with free will, led him down a path that brought death into the world.

Moving forward to Avraham Avinu. Nurture would have dictated that he follow his father Terach into idol worship. His father manufactured and sold idols, so Avraham was literally raised in a house and business built on avodah zarah. He could have followed his father either into belief in false gods or into the cynical business of selling them. Yet Avraham broke free entirely. He used his bechirah, his free will, to recognize truth and forge a new path. This teaches us that while nature and nurture may influence us profoundly, they do not determine our destiny. The bechirah given to Adam and passed down to all humanity allows us to transcend our circumstances.

Rivka: A Rose Among Thorns

We see this perhaps most dramatically in Rivka. She was raised by Betuel and Lavan, not exactly paragons of virtue. The mefarshim explain that these were people so corrupt that they tried to poison Eliezer while he was in their home, hoping to steal his wealth. Her mother Milcah went along with their schemes. These were people characterized by deception, greed, and violence.

Even more disturbing, Chazal teach that when Rivka chose to leave with Eliezer to marry Yitzchak, she wanted to depart with great haste because the region where she lived was known as a place where children were violated. It was spiritually and morally dangerous in the extreme.

On one level, we might say it is only natural to want to escape such a place. But consider the nurture aspect. This was her reality, her normal. We see with Lot that when he tried to warn his sons in law about the impending destruction of Sodom, they thought he was joking. They could not conceive of leaving because the evil had become normalized to them. Many people do not recognize they need to leave toxic environments because those environments have shaped their entire worldview.

But Rivka's personal awareness, even at a young age, told her clearly that this is a bad place to be and these are not the values she wants to live by.

Questions for Reflection

How am I uplifting the Imahot in my world? Whether they are mothers now, will become mothers, or are not able to become mothers (chas v’shalom), how am I ensuring that the women around me are treated with respect and dignity?

Second: How am I breaking out of my own patterns of nature and nurture to become an even more exemplary human being? Even if we were raised in righteous homes, we can always grow further. How can I push beyond what was given to me to reach higher levels of holiness and service?

Third: How am I enabling those around me to grow beyond their seeming limitations? How can I uplift others, like Eliezer, helping them rise above their circumstances and step into their mission in the eyes of Hashem?

Have a wonderful, blessed Shabbat.

Dvar Torah for Parshas Toldos

Building Toldos with Awareness, Mesorah, and Responsibility

Parshas Toldos opens with a verse that at first glance seems simple, yet it contains a deep and powerful teaching about who we are and how we shape the future. The Torah says: אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת יִצְחָק בֶּן אַבְרָהָם. אַבְרָהָם הוֹלִיד אֶת יִצְחָק “These are the generations of Yitzchak son of Avraham. Avraham fathered Yitzchak.”

Every word in the Torah has purpose. Every nekudah carries value. By introducing Yitzchak through Avraham, the Torah teaches that Toldos are not only about what emerges from me in the future, but also about the forces and people that shaped me from the past. Toldos are not merely descendants. Toldos is identity unfolding forward. Toldos is a contious path, where each step forward carries the awareness of what came before and the intention of what will come after. It is legacy. It is the continuation of something that began before me and continues through me.

Beginning with Creation: Toldos HaShamayim VehaAretz

To understand this deeply, we return to the first appearance of the word in the Torah. In Bereishis 2:4 the Torah states: אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְהָאָרֶץ בְּהִבָּרְאָם “These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created.”

This appears after creation is complete. The world already contains everything required for ongoing development. HaShem embedded within reality the seeds of continuation. Even creation has Toldos, but unlike the first act of yesh miayin, the Toldos of creation unfold naturally, moving forward from what came before.

The Torah uses the same structure with Noach. אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ “These are the generations of Noach.” We then see Shem, Cham, and Yefes, the division of lands, and the forming of nations. Toldos is not a single moment. It is the movement of potential into form, and form into legacy.

Toldos in Our Lives: Active or Passive

We often associate Toldos with children, but Toldos also describes who I become because of those who shaped me. A father, teacher, friend, mentor, and community all generate Toldos. My past gives rise to my present. My present will give rise to someone else’s future.

Mesorah מסורה teaches this. Some people hold their mesorah with awe. Others take it for granted. Yet the Torah insists that the first step in building my future is asking: Where did I come from, and where am I going.

Toldos in Halacha: The Rambam’s Definition

The Rambam, in his commentary to the Mishnah, Shabbos 7:2, defines a toladah תולדה as an act similar in result to one of the av melachot אבות מלאכה, but different in its method, intent, or manner. The outcome resembles the av, even though the expression is new. This halachic definition mirrors the Torah’s idea of Toldos. Children do not replicate their parents. Students do not become identical to their teachers. Generations do not copy what came before. Instead, each generation continues the essence through new forms. The core stays the same. The vessel changes.

Mesorah is not duplication. Mesorah is continuation. It is the passing of the original light through new prisms and into new vessels. Toldos means that what came before continues through me with my unique strengths, circumstances, and choices. The essence remains consistent. The expression evolves. This is as true in halacha as it is in life.

Avraham, Yitzchak, and the Conscious Choice to Create Toldos

People often say that any man can be a father, but it takes a man to be a dad. In the Torah, to be holid הוֹלִיד means purposeful involvement. It means choosing to build something that will outlive me. Avraham holid es Yitzchak. Avraham shaped Yitzchak with presence and intention. Yitzchak, known for his gevurah גבורה, held himself with discipline and clarity. He partnered with Rivka, established a home of purpose, and continued Avraham’s mission with HaShem as the third partner.

Toldos does not happen by accident. Toldos is created with kavvanah and intention.

The Balance of Yaakov: Tiferes Gives Birth to Greatness

Kabbalah teaches that Avraham is chessed חסד, Yitzchak is gevurah, and Yaakov is tiferes תפארת, the harmonious balance between the two. Because Yaakov embodies this balance, he expands beyond both of them. His children become the Shevatim. His Toldos become the foundation of Am Yisrael.

Before building his home, Yaakov immerses himself in the yeshiva of Shem and Ever. Chazal explain that he pauses to strengthen his mesorah before building the future. He asks the essential question of Toldos: To know who I must become, I must first know where I come from.

Toldos in Hashkafah: Creating with Intention

Halacha distinguishes between intentional outcomes and nolad נולד, something born unintentionally. This distinction mirrors our spiritual work. Do my actions create intentional Toldos, rooted in mesorah and identity. Or do they drift into accidental outcomes without direction.

This contrast appears again with Bilam. The Torah says: וַיִּקָּר אֱלֹקים אֶל בִּלְעָם, “HaShem happened upon Bilam.” Rashi notes the contrast with Moshe’s nevuah נבואה: וַיִּקְרָא, “HaShem called.”

Moshe experiences a relationship. Bilam experiences coincidence. Moshe represents intentional Toldos. Bilam represents accidental outcomes.

The Midrash on Toldos Noach: Fruits of the Tzadikim

Bereishis Rabbah comments on אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדֹת נֹחַ with the teaching: עיקר תולדותיהם של צדיקים מעשים טובים “The primary offspring of the righteous are their good deeds.”

Our Toldos are not only our children. They are our maasim מעשים, our dibburim דיבורים, our machshavos מחשבות, and our middos. The Maharal in Gevuros HaShem explains that every mitzvah performed through machshavah, dibbur, and maaseh creates spiritual Toldos that ascend through all the worlds. The opposite also generates forces that bring din.

Mesorah: Connecting Past and Future

The Baal Shem Tov teaches that a Jew must know the root of his soul. Mesorah is the unbroken chain connecting what was to what will be. When we act with awareness, we stand inside this chain. When we act without awareness, we step outside it. Pirkei Avos says: הֱוֵי מִתְאַבֵּק בַּעֲפַר רַגְלֵיהֶם, “Sit in the dust of the feet of the sages.”

This teaches humility and listening, even when the tzadik or chacham does not appear as expected. With healthy gevurah we accept what is good and reject what is not. This too is Toldos.

A Shabbos of Toldos

As we enter Shabbos we can ask ourselves: What came before me. Who am I because of those actions? What actions can I take now to shape the world? Are my next steps rooted in my mesorah? Am I creating true Toldos?

Most importantly: Am I a clear and balanced reflection of tiferes, the harmony of chessed and gevurah, like Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov.

May we merit to build generations of goodness, actions that ripple forward, and Toldos that carry the mission of our Avos into the future.

A beautiful Shabbos, everybody.

D'var Torah on Parshas Vayetzei: When Speech Builds and Listening Unites

Foundational Themes

Parshas Vayetzei is a parsha of transition. The Torah opens, "ויצא יעקב מבאר שבע וילך חרנה" (Bereishis 28:10). Yaakov leaves Be'er Sheva and walks toward Charan, a movement not only of place but of identity. Yaakov Avinu leaves his parents' home, leaves safety, and steps into exile. This is where the Jewish people are first formed: not in holiness, not in comfort, but inside complexity.

Beneath the storyline of journeys, marriages, and rivalries lies a deeper theme: the power of letters, words, speech, and listening. Not just communication but relationship. Not just words but unity. Not just expression but connection.

The Power of Conversation

Earlier this week, I had a long conversation with one of my mashpi'im about something simple yet profound, : when one person speaks continuously without leaving space for the other to respond, even without bad intention, the result can become harmful. Real dialogue requires exchange—one speaks, one listens, and then they trade places. This back-and-forth is not just conversation; it is the foundation of building and maintaining relationships.

Speech without space can collapse connection. Listening without voice can erase identity.

Health lives in balance. And that is one of the lessons Parshas Vayetzei shows us.

Leaving and Being Felt

When Yaakov leaves Be'er Sheva, Chazal teach that the city feels his absence. This is learned from the extra wording of "ויצא יעקב מבאר שבע" (Bereishis 28:10)—the Torah highlights his departure because it mattered. There is a difference between someone whose departure brings relief and someone whose departure leaves emptiness.

There are people who leave, and things breathe easier. There are people who leave, and the room goes quiet.

Yaakov was the second kind.

The Torah teaches us something powerful: it is not only who you are when you arrive that matters, it is who you are when you leave. Or as the Baal Shem Tov taught us to reflect: "What would people say at your funeral?"

The Stones and the Letters

Then comes the night, and Yaakov lies down.

The Torah says, "ויקח מאבני המקום" (Bereishis 28:11)—he took from the stones of the place. Later, after the dream, the Torah says, "ויקח את האבן" (Bereishis 28:18)—he took the stone, in the singular.

Rashi (Bereishis 28:11) describes the scene beautifully:

Hebrew: "התחילו מריבות זו עם זו, זאת אומרת עלי יניח צדיק את ראשו, וזאת אומרת עלי יניח, מיד עשאן הקדוש ברוך הוא אבן אחת"

English: "The stones began arguing with one another. Each one said, 'Let the righteous one rest his head upon me.' Immediately, Hashem made them into one stone, turning rivalry into unity."

Kabbalah and Chassidus take this further. The Alter Rebbe brings a teaching from Sefer Yetzirah (Perek 4:12):

שתי אבנים בונות שתי בתים. שלש אבנים בונות שש בתים. ארבע אבנים בונות עשרים וארבעה בתים.

In English: Two stones build two houses. Three stones build six houses. Four stones build twenty-four houses.

The stones are not just stones—they are letters. Letters combine, words form, and reality multiplies. The more letters, the more combinations possible, bringing more words, more speech, and the ability to build more worlds.

But Yaakov's stones move in the opposite direction: not from one to many, but from many to one. Not multiplication, but unification.

The message is striking. Words can build worlds, but they can also fracture them. When speech is fragmented, relationships crumble. When speech is unified, holiness enters. This doesn't mean all speech needs to be the same—it means there is space for all speech to exist in the same space.

Three Styles of Speech

Now compare Yaakov to his father and grandfather.

Avraham spoke outward. He challenged the world. He argued with Hashem for good. He brought strangers into his tent and pulled ideas into the light.

Yitzchak spoke inward. He was formed through silence. The Akeidah is quiet. His tefillah is private. He does not fight reality; he accepts it. When he discovers it was Yaakov who received the brachos, he doesn't protest or give additional blessings—he accepts what has unfolded.

Yaakov speaks between people. He negotiates. He explains. He listens. He creates relationship through conversation.

The Art of Listening

Yaakov's greatness is not only in how he speaks, but in how he listens.

He listens to Rivkah when she tells him to take the brachah (Bereishis 27:8–10) and when she sends him to her family in Charan (Bereishis 27:43). He listens to Rachel and Leah before leaving Lavan, and only moves after hearing them (Bereishis 31:4–16). He listens to Yosef's dreams—"ואביו שמר את הדבר" (Bereishis 37:11), he guarded the matter. He listens to Lavan, even when wronged, until there comes a moment when truth must finally speak.

And later, standing before Paroh (Bereishis 47:8–9), the most powerful man on earth, Paroh asks him a simple question: "How many are the days of your life?"

Yaakov gives no performance. No flattery. No politics.

He answers from truth: "מעט ורעים היו ימי שני חיי" (Bereishis 47:9).

"My life was hard." "Few were my days." "I did not reach my fathers."

That is a man who has listened to his own story.

From Noise to Meaning

Avraham changed the world with speech. Yitzchak deepened the soul with silence. Yaakov built a nation through conversation.

He teaches us that holiness does not live in volume or withdrawal. It lives in relationship: listening with intention—what Rabbi Gerzi calls "Baal Shem Tov listening"—speaking with care, and answering with honesty.

Shabbos as a Return to Dialogue

Shabbos invites us into what Yaakov mastered.

We turn off the noise. We put down distance. We undo fracture.

We speak. We listen. We reconnect.

Not as performers. Not as commentators. As people.

As family. As Jews.

Reflection and Growth

This week, ask yourself:

● Am I speaking for my own needs, or speaking to build relationship with those I am speaking with?

● Am I listening in order to answer, or listening in order to receive?

● Do my words build space, or do they take it?

● Am I arguing to win, or communicating to connect?

Closing Thought

Many letters can build many worlds. But unity builds eternity.

Gut Shabbos
