He wasn't overly outgoing, he wasn't too quiet and shut in—he was able to balance it out.

Avraham—we see that while he was speaking outwards, in a good way, he was able to spread the message, to reach out to those around him. He was known for being a little bit argumentative with Hashem—outward speaking about Hashem's message, very outwardly. But not necessarily to people who were able to be permanently in a long-winded kavannah. It's almost like that situation my mashpia and I were speaking about—speaking in a continuous way that others can't respond. It's being a force alongside a relationship.

Yitzchak—by the Akeidah, was a very quiet person, asked simple questions. He was very simplistic in his words, doesn't say very much. When he figures out, after the fact, that it was Yaakov who got the bracha, instead of saying, ah, let me give you more brachos anyways—because we are zocheh to give essentially infinite bracha—he held himself back: I don't have more bracha right now, not on this. He was able to listen and be mekabel on the reality surrounding him. He was very aware of everything, but he didn't say much. He didn't push outwards in that same way.

Yaakov—his speech and his mannerism of communication, his choice of how he would use words and letters. Even when his own father was essentially blinded, and he was wearing a costume pretending to be somebody else, it was impossible for him to completely fool his father, because his way of speech was so refined.

We see the way that he speaks. His brother Eisav was also quite specific in his words, but in a very different way. Yaakov was able to purchase the birthright, the right of being a bechor. Eisav's choice of words was: "Pour that soup down my throat"—not the cleanest or nicest way of speaking. Yaakov's response was: "Okay, well, if this is what you really want, then I really want something in return. And here's what it is." And he describes what makes a bechor, he describes the gevurah, the responsibility involved. Elegant words, truthful words.

The Art of Listening

Yaakov speaks between people. He negotiates. He explains. He listens. He creates relationship through conversation.

He speaks with his wives and listens to them, asking their opinions, their perspectives. Towards the end of this week's Parsha, when he takes his wives into the field to discuss their getaway plan, he asks their input, and they don't hold back. He listens to them speaking through what is taking place—their reality, their awareness of their father, and everything else going on around them.

We see over and over again his conversations with his children. How he sits, how he speaks, and how he listens. The beauty of listening. Not everyone has that gift. Not everyone can sit and listen to their friends around them. Not everyone can sit and listen to their own dreams.

One example of the ability to listen and sit is we will see, coming up, how Yosef describes his dreams to his father. His father is able to sit and listen in detail as his son communicates, and to have an exchange around it. "ואביו שמר את הדבר" (Bereishis 37:11)—he guarded the matter. He wasn't listening with the intent of responding, he was listening with the intent of listening. As Rabbi Gerzi calls this, "Baal Shem Tov listening." I'm going to put myself to the side for this moment, while I listen to what the other side has to give. And based on their needs for me, I will give a response.

In this week's Parsha, we see this so strongly. We see how he was able to sit and listen to Lavan's requirements as they're negotiating the terms of employment. And then renegotiating in the later stages, by the trickery with Leah and then Rachel. He was able to communicate and interact with Lavan after they leave, and Lavan catches up with them and gives him such a hard time. And Yaakov also knows that sometimes there's a time to stand your ground, to speak strongly, based on reality and your values. After letting Lavan vent, he essentially had enough of disrespect towards himself and his wives. He explains to Lavan all the pain and trickery he had caused, saying enough is enough, because now I'm out from underneath your shadow. But while in there, he was always being respectful, which is why Lavan was able to get away with it for so long.

And later, standing before Paroh (Bereishis 47:8–9), the most powerful man on earth, Paroh asks him a simple question: "How many are the days of your life?"

Yaakov gives no performance. No flattery. No politics.

He answers from truth: "מעט ורעים היו ימי שני חיי" (Bereishis 47:9).

"My life was hard." "Few were my days." "I did not reach my fathers."

That is a man who has listened to his own story.

From Noise to Meaning

Avraham changed the world with speech. Yitzchak deepened the soul with silence. Yaakov built a nation through conversation.

Yaakov's ability to speak, to communicate, and to have this bi-directional reality—this would be amongst those things that made him the right person, that we then become named after him, because we're Bnei Yisrael, and Yaakov becomes Yisrael.

He teaches us that holiness does not live in volume or withdrawal. It lives in relationship: listening with intention—"Baal Shem Tov listening"—speaking with care, and answering with honesty.

Shabbos as a Return to Dialogue

As we go into Shabbos, the world has in some ways quieted down around us, in some ways it's getting even louder. It gives us this beautiful opportunity to reflect as we unplug from the world, unplug from the long distance, from the internet.

We can sit and utilize this time to, as Bnei Yisrael, communicate, to listen to each other, to share words of love and compassion, to be the people who are zocheh that every day we get to be the ones who are mekadesh by the choice of being with these people. What makes me who I am today, I come from them.

We speak. We listen. We reconnect.

Not as performers. Not as commentators. As people.

As family. As Jews.

Reflection and Growth

It's a beautiful thing to learn: When is it the time to be outgoing and flamboyant, and to spread a loud message? When is it the time to sit and be quiet? And when is it the time to be the Yaakov, and to converse, and to have full dialogue and back-and-forth conversation, with a goal of growth and prosperity, and to be able to love each other in this way?

This week, ask yourself:

● Am I speaking for my own needs, or speaking to build relationship with those I am speaking with?

● Am I listening in order to answer, or listening in order to receive?

● Do my words build space, or do they take it?

● Am I arguing to win, or communicating to connect?

Closing Thought

Many letters can build many worlds. But unity builds eternity.

Have an amazing, beautiful Shabbos.

D’var Torah on Parshas Vayetzei: When Speech Builds and Listening Unites

Foundational Themes

Parshas Vayetzei is a parsha of transition. The Torah opens, "ויצא יעקב מבאר שבע וילך חרנה" (Bereishis 28:10), Yaakov leaves Be’er Sheva and walks toward Charan, a movement not only of place but of identity. Yaakov Avinu leaves his parents’ home, leaves safety, and steps into exile. This is where the Jewish people are first formed not in holiness, not in comfort, but inside complexity.

But beneath the storyline of journeys, marriages, and rivalries lies a deeper theme that runs through the parsha: the power of letters, words, speaking, listening and communicating.

And not just communication, but relationship. Not just words, but unity. Not just expression, but connection.

The Power of Conversation

Earlier this week, I was zocheh to have a long conversation with one of my mashpi’im about the value of conversation and the importance of words. We spoke about something simple yet profound.

When one person speaks continuously and never leaves space for the other to respond, even without bad intention, the result can become harmful. Real dialogue requires exchange. One speaks, one listens, and then they trade places. This back and forth is not just conversation, it is the start and foundation of building and maintaining relationships.

Speech without space can collapse connection. Listening without voice can erase identity.

Health lives in balance. And it was such perfect timing to have that conversation during this week’s Parsha Vayetzei.

And that is at least one of the lessons which Parshas Vayetzei shows us.

Leaving and Being Felt

When Yaakov leaves Be’er Sheva, Chazal teach that the city feels his absence, learned from the extra wording of "ויצא יעקב מבאר שבע" (Bereishis 28:10), that the Torah highlights his departure because it mattered. There is a difference between someone whose departure brings relief and someone whose departure leaves emptiness.

There are people who leave, and things breathe easier. There are people who leave, and the room goes quiet.

Yaakov was the second kind.

The Torah teaches us something powerful here: it is not only who you are when you arrive that matters, it is who you are when you leave. Or as the Baal Shem Tov taught us to ask ourselves, "What would people say at your funeral?"

The Stones and the Letters

Then comes the night and Yaakov lies down.

The Torah says, "ויקח מאבני המקום" (Bereishis 28:11), he took from the stones of the place and lay down. Later, after the dream, the Torah says, "ויקח את האבן" (Bereishis 28:18), he took the stone, in the singular.

Rashi (Bereishis 28:11) describes the scene with beautiful imagery:

Hebrew: "התחילו מריבות זו עם זו, זאת אומרת עלי יניח צדיק את ראשו, וזאת אומרת עלי יניח, מיד עשאן הקדוש ברוך הוא אבן אחת"

English: "The stones began arguing with one another. Each one said, 'Let the righteous one rest his head upon me.' Immediately, Hashem made them into one stone, turning rivalry into unity."

Kabbalah and Chassidus take this further.

The Alter Rebbe in a maamar on the power of speech and malchus for this week’s parsha brings a teaching from Sefer Yetzirah (Perek 4:12): שתי אבנים בונות שתי בתים. שלש אבנים בונות שש בתים. ארבע אבנים עשרים וארבעה בתים.

Two stones build two houses. Three stones build six houses. Four stones build twenty four houses.

The stones are not just stones. They are letters. When you have two letters, you have two combinations. When you have three letters, the possible words increase.

Letters combine, words form and reality multiplies. The more letters there are, the more combinations are possible which bring more words, more speech and the ability to build more worlds.

But Yaakov’s stones move in the opposite direction.

Not from one to many, from many to one. Not multiplication but rather unification.

The message is striking. Words can build worlds but they can also fracture them. When speech is fragmented, relationships crumble. When speech is unified, holiness enters. This doesn't mean that all the speech needs to be the same, it means that there is space for all the speech to exist in the same space in a respectful way.

Three Styles of Speech

Now compare Yaakov to his father and grandfather.

Avraham spoke outward. He challenged the world. He argued with Hashem (for good things). He brought strangers into his tent and pulled ideas into the light.

Yitzchak spoke inward. He was formed through silence. The Akeidah is quiet. His tefillah is private. He does not fight reality, he accepts it.

And Yaakov? Yaakov speaks between people. He negotiates. He explains. He listens. He creates relationships through conversation.

The Art of Listening

Yaakov’s greatness is not only in how he speaks, but in how he listens.

He listens to Rivkah when she tells him to take the brachah (Bereishis 27:8–10) and when she sends him to her family in Charan (Bereishis 27:43). He listens to Rachel and Leah before leaving Lavan, and only moves after hearing them (Bereishis 31:4–16). He listens to Yosef’s dreams and "ואביו שמר את הדבר" (Bereishis 37:11), he guarded the matter. He listens to Lavan, even when wronged, until there comes a moment when truth must finally speak.

And later, standing before Paroh (Bereishis 47:8–9),, the most powerful man on earth, Paroh asks him a simple question:

“How many are the days of your life?”

Yaakov gives no performance. No flattery. No politics.

He answers from truth, "מעט ורעים היו ימי שני חיי" (Bereishis 47:9).

“My life was hard.” “Few were my days.” “I did not reach my fathers.”

That is a man who has listened to his own story.

From Noise to Meaning

Avraham changed the world with speech. Yitzchak deepened the soul with silence. Yaakov built a nation through conversation.

He teaches us that holiness does not live in volume or withdrawal. It lives in relationship: listening with intention, what Rabbi Gerzi calls "Baal Shem Tov listening," speaking with care, and answering with honesty. It lives in relationship. Listening with intention as Rabbi Gerzi call this "Baal Shem Tov listening". From there speaking with care and answering with honesty.

Shabbos as a Return to Dialogue

Shabbos invites us into what Yaakov mastered.

We turn off the noise. We put down distance. We undo fracture.

We speak. We listen. We reconnect.

Not as performers. Not as commentators. As people.

As family. As Jews.

Reflection and Growth

This week, ask yourself:

● Am I speaking for just my own needs or speaking to build more relationship with those I am speaking with?

● Am I listening in order to answer, or listening in order to receive?

● Do my words build space, or do they take it?

● Am I arguing to win, or communicating to connect?

Closing Thought

Many letters can build many worlds. But unity builds eternity.

D'var Torah on Parshas Vayishlach: Standing in Front

Introduction: The Unique Message of Every Parsha

This week's Parsha, Parshas Vayishlach, has a profound message. Obviously, I say that about every Parsha, every Chag. And it's very much true, every single time. Because each Parsha has a unique message, and each time you read it, the message will be different, hopefully growing and enhancing with every step of the way.

The journey of Torah study is one of constant renewal. Each reading brings new depth, new understanding, new relevance to our lives.

The Meaning of Vayishlach: Sending Forward

The word Vayishlach means "and he sent out." The Torah opens with this word (Bereishis 32:4): "וישלח יעקב מלאכים לפניו אל עשו אחיו," And Yaakov sent messengers ahead of him to Eisav his brother.

The flow of this week's Parsha, and quite often in life, means we're sending something forward of us. In this situation, you see that Yaakov sends out malachim to check in on his brother, to do the best of his ability to ensure that he would have safety.

But there's a deeper question here: Why now? Why is Yaakov ready to face Eisav at this particular moment?

The Prerequisite: Yosef's Birth

If you look at last week's Parsha, when Yaakov prepares to leave Lavan, the Torah tells us (Bereishis 30:25): "ויהי כאשר ילדה רחל את יוסף," And it was when Rachel gave birth to Yosef. Rashi explains on this pasuk that it wasn't until Yosef was born that Yaakov was ready to leave and eventually face Eisav.

Why? Because Yosef was the only one who would have the koach to take on Eisav. The Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 73:7) teaches that Yosef is compared to fire, while Eisav is compared to straw: "והיה בית יעקב אש ובית יוסף להבה ובית עשו לקש," The house of Yaakov will be fire, the house of Yosef a flame, and the house of Eisav like straw (Ovadiah 1:18).

Now that Yaakov has Yosef, now that he has the one who can spiritually take on Eisav, he sends out scouts, he sends out malachim to look at the reality of the situation before any confrontation comes. This is strategic preparation, gathering intelligence before action.

The Terrifying Message

And what message do the malachim bring back? The Torah records (Bereishis 32:7): "וישבו המלאכים אל יעקב לאמר באנו אל אחיך אל עשו וגם הלך לקראתך וארבע מאות איש עמו," The messengers returned to Yaakov saying, "We came to your brother, to Eisav, and he is also coming toward you, and four hundred men are with him."

"Sir, I have some good news and some bad news. The good news is that your brother wants to see you. The bad news is it's because he wants to kill you. And he has an army 400 strong." It's a terrifying message to receive.

The Torah continues (Bereishis 32:8): "וַיִּירָא יַעֲקֹב מְאֹד וַיֵּצֶר לוֹ," And Yaakov became very frightened and distressed. Rashi explains the double language: he was frightened that he might be killed, and distressed that he might have to kill others.

Now, Rashi, who always goes with the simplest explanation, the pshat, says that these malachim were literally angels, not any other sort of messenger. But when we look at the messaging here, what happened? Is it that Yaakov sent out malachim to keep himself safe? No. He sent out malachim to see and to scope out the situation, to gather information.

The Three-Pronged Approach

Yaakov's response to the threat is methodical and comprehensive. The mefashim teach that Yaakov prepared himself in three ways: "בשלשה דברים תיקן עצמו: בדורון, בתפילה, ובמלחמה," In three things he prepared himself: with gifts, with prayer, and with war.

The Torah describes each of these preparations in detail. First, the gifts (Bereishis 32:14-21), carefully selected and sent in waves to appease Eisav. Second, the prayer (Bereishis 32:10-13), where Yaakov calls out to Hashem: "הצילני נא מיד אחי מיד עשו כי ירא אנכי אתו," Save me please from the hand of my brother, from the hand of Eisav, for I fear him. And third, the preparation for war, dividing his camp so that at least some would survive.

But the most crucial moment comes not in planning, but in action.

Wrestling with the Angel: A Test of Strength

As we move forward in the Parsha, something extraordinary happens. A man wrestles with Yaakov all night long. The Torah describes (Bereishis 32:25-26): "ויאבק איש עמו עד עלות השחר. וירא כי לא יכל לו," And a man wrestled with him until the break of dawn. And when he saw that he could not prevail against him.

Rashi explains that this "man" was the ministering angel of Eisav, the spiritual force behind Eisav's physical power. The wrestling match wasn't just physical; it was spiritual warfare. And Yaakov prevailed.

The angel then says (Bereishis 32:27): "שלחני כי עלה השחר," Send me away, for dawn has broken. But Yaakov refuses to let go without a blessing. The angel responds by changing his name (Bereishis 32:29): "לא יעקב יאמר עוד שמך כי אם ישראל כי שרית עם אלקים ועם אנשים ותוכל," No longer will your name be called Yaakov, but Yisrael, for you have struggled with the divine and with men, and you have prevailed.

This is the moment of transformation. Yaakov becomes Yisrael. He has the bracha, he has the strength, he has prevailed over the angel of Eisav himself. He is ready.

Standing in Front: The Ultimate Leadership

And now comes the moment of truth. When Yaakov finally meets his brother, the Torah tells us something powerful (Bereishis 33:3): "והוא עבר לפניהם," And he passed before them.

Yaakov's priorities and his realities were clear. Even knowing he has a bracha from Hashem, even knowing he got a bracha from an enemy angel that he was able to fight, even knowing his strength and his balance, he also knows his brother wants to kill him. And what does he do?

He doesn't hide behind his wives. He doesn't hide behind his children. He doesn't send someone else forward. Instead, he stands in front of everybody else. He went in front.

It's no longer a situation of vayishlach, that he sends forward somebody else. The time for sending scouts has passed. The time for preparation is over. Now is the time for action, for leadership, for standing at the head.

It's not just a level of mesiras nefesh, a willingness to give up one's life. He's ready to stand and fight. The Midrashim teach: if someone needs to fall, that'll be me. But not that I want to fall instead of anybody else. I'm going to be here, I'm going to go forward, I'm going to stand straight. I know what to fight for.

Rashi brings another beautiful insight on the words "והוא עבר לפניהם," explaining that Yaakov bowed seven times as he approached his brother, corresponding to the seven times the word "אדוני," my master, appears in his message to Eisav. He humbled himself, but he stood in front. He led with dignity and with strategy.

The Precedent of Avraham: Fighting for Values

We see this pattern earlier in our history. By Avraham, when he went to fight to liberate Lot (Bereishis 14:14-16), the Torah records: "וישמע אברם כי נשבה אחיו," And Avram heard that his kinsman was taken captive. What follows is a military campaign to rescue Lot from the four kings who had captured him.

The Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 41:6) explains something fascinating: what was Avraham really fighting for? Was it just Lot? According to this Midrash, Avraham and Lot looked identical, or nearly identical. And so what was Avraham fighting for?

He was fighting for his own value system and his name. If they had succeeded in breaking Lot and getting Lot to go back to serving avodah zarah and then dying in that state, the word would have spread around the world that Avraham had failed. Because even though it wasn't Avraham, they looked the same.

Avraham would stand up and fight for what was right, even if he would fall in the process. Better that he would fall in battle, and everyone knows the truth, than to have Lot fall after giving in to avodah zarah and have everybody think that Avraham and his message stood for nothing.

This is the legacy of our Avos: standing up for values, for truth, for what is right, even at great personal risk.

Throughout Our History: Leaders Who Stood in Front

We see so many times throughout Tanach, we see it in stories of the Gemara, about Jews, about Yidden, about Bnei Yisrael, willing to put up the fight. Sometimes it's a verbal fight. Sometimes it's a physical fight. But always, the leader stands at the head.

Moshe Rabbeinu put himself out there as the head when Hashem wanted to wipe out Bnei Yisrael after the sin of the Golden Calf. The Torah records his prayer (Shemos 32:32): "ועתה אם תשא חטאתם ואם אין מחני נא מספרך אשר כתבת," And now, if You would forgive their sin, and if not, erase me now from Your book that You have written.

He said, "No, I'm not going to take over for them. I'm not going to replace them. Remove me from Your book as well. You will wipe out my name if You're going to take out these people." This is leadership: standing with your people, not above them.

The head, the rosh, the leader, knows that they're supposed to be leading by being at the head. We all live our lives this way. We lead our life by our head. At first, we use our head, we use our brain, and we make sure that takes precedence.

Esther HaMalka prepared herself to go before the king, where people would die every time for appearing uninvited, including her own predecessor, Queen Vashti. The Megillah records (Esther 4:16): "וכאשר אבדתי אבדתי," And if I perish, I perish. She went in ready to fight for her people, by standing in charge, by taking control, knowing that her job as a leader was to do these things.

Mordechai HaTzaddik, we see as well, was willing to stand up and give up his life instead of bowing before the wicked Haman. The Megillah tells us (Esther 3:2): "ומרדכי לא יכרע ולא ישתחוה," But Mordechai would not kneel or bow. When questioned, he stood firm in his principles, knowing it could cost him his life.

The Chashmonaim during the time of Chanukah stood up, saying, "No, I'm not going to give in to the Greeks. I will do what is right." They were few against many, weak against strong, but they stood at the head and led the Jewish people back to Torah and to Hashem.

And in today's world, too, we see where Bnei Yisrael is willing to fight for their values, fight for what is right, and to know that they, as individuals, need to stand there and be a strong leader.

As a head, I'm supposed to be in front of my body. I'm supposed to lead with my head and keep the rest of me safe. It seems almost contradictory, but it is a true statement: by placing ourselves in front, by taking the risk, we actually protect what is most precious to us.

A Lesson from the Street: Instinctual Protection

I want to share a small story. The idea behind the story is not to be degrading towards this person, but there's wisdom and insight that we can learn from our own responses, our own natural responses to the world around us.

The other day, I was walking my dog. There was a woman walking with her husband, pushing a stroller. Now, most parents, almost all parents, would give up their lives for their children. This woman, seeing my dog, jumped behind the stroller to put the stroller, really put her baby, in between my dog and herself.

Now, those who know my dog know her better. She weighs about eight and a half pounds, 4.1 kilos. She is not much. And she's old, she's missing about half of her teeth. This woman doesn't know that my dog doesn't have all her teeth, or that she's old.

But an instinct inside of her, the instinct of the average parent to be most beneficial to their child's life, to keep their children safe, something that we gain from the middos of the Avos. Part of those middos of the Avos we've spoken about, by Avraham, by Yitzchak, by Yaakov, is knowing how to give up ourselves to ensure everything afterwards goes forward.

But here's the fascinating thing: her instinct wasn't quite right, was it? She put her child in front of her, not behind her. She didn't stand between the perceived threat and her child; she put her child between herself and the threat.

But maybe her instinct was that far off.

There is something inside of us that is usually able to help us understand the difference, even if not logical, between what may kill that next generation versus what may harm. This is a deeper wisdom, a gift from Hashem.

As a parent, I never want my children to get hurt. An unfortunate reality of growing up is that people do get hurt. Children hit their heads on things. Hopefully, they're wearing a helmet if they're riding a bicycle. People who know me well know that I rant about helmet safety, and I have a dream of one day driving around with helmets just to hand them out to children, and even more so to adults who don't set a good example.

But we know that getting hurt, being harmed in life, is a reality. People get hurt. Our children get hurt. And God willing, they come out stronger because of it. That's the reason why we allow our children to walk, to run, to ride bicycles, to play games, and to learn how to do things. Because if we keep them completely coddled at all times and prevent them from ever getting hurt physically in any way, shape, or form, they can never grow.

The Gemara in Sotah (46b) teaches: "עולם כמנהגו נוהג," The world follows its natural course. Part of that natural course includes challenge, includes difficulty, includes the minor injuries of childhood that teach resilience and strength.

But instinctually, I know the difference between something where my child may get hurt versus my child will die. And the ability to then step forward and say, "No, I'm going to do my best to make sure that I survive whatever the fallout may be right now. But you are not going to end the life of my child. You are not going to stop or break that which I hold most precious and dear to me."

Whether that be a child, a belief structure, Torah, mitzvos, we have that within us as a gift from Hashem, a natural response of our neshama. Maybe even also a chelek of a higher insight that we get as being part of Bnei Yisrael.

This insight, this higher level, this is what tells us: I need to stand in front. My child may get smacked a little bit, but they're going to come out of this.

And kol hakavod to that woman who jumped to the other side of her child. There's something inside of her that knew no one's going to die, no one's going to get that badly hurt, and it's okay. Her instinct, even if her positioning was off, was fundamentally correct: assess the threat, and respond accordingly.

Refining Our Middos and Our Bodies

We all get to learn to listen to ourselves, to that inner wisdom. As Rabbi Gerzi teaches, we've been talking about our middos, we've been talking about our guf, our body. Our guf can also be responding to our middos.

The Alter Rebbe teaches in Tanya (Chapter 1) that the nefesh habahamis, the animal soul, is clothed in the blood and in the physical body. But as we refine our middos, as we work on ourselves spiritually, this has an impact on the physical as well.

As those of us who learn from Rabbi Gerzi learn as well, the more we grow, the more we change and impact our middos and refine them, the more that will then have an impact on our body. Our body becomes this more natural responsive engine that learns how to do the ratzon of Hashem. And then from that, that's going to bring our middos to a higher level as well which will then bring our body even higher yet.

It's a cycle of growth: spiritual refinement leads to physical refinement, which enables deeper spiritual refinement. The body and soul work together, each elevating the other.

Tying It All Together: The Name of the Parsha

We can tie all this back to the name of the Parsha: Vayishlach, "and he sent out."

He sent out for information. Why? To prepare himself, his middos, which were then able to prepare his guf. He was able to be working on his natural state of survival, and to say, "No, the survival of me as an individual doesn't matter as much as that which I hold most dear, that which I'm going to hold behind me."

So he was able to send forward those who gathered information. But when it came time to do, when it came time to potentially fight, to stand up for what is correct, Yaakov was able to do so.

He stood in front. He led with his head. He protected what was behind him.

The progression is clear:

Vayishlach - Send out scouts, gather information, prepare

Vaye'avek - Struggle and wrestle with challenges, gain strength

Vaya'avor lifneihem - Pass before them, stand in front, lead

This is the model for our own lives. We prepare, we struggle and grow through that struggle, and then we stand up and lead. We protect what matters most by placing ourselves at the head, by being willing to face the threat directly.

The Deeper Message: Knowing When to Stand

But there's an even deeper lesson here. Yaakov didn't always stand in front. For twenty years with Lavan, he bent, he accommodated, he accepted injustice. Why? Because the time wasn't right. He was building, preparing, growing his family.

Now, with his family behind him, with Yosef born, with the bracha from the angel, the time has come to stand. The time has come to say: enough. No more running. No more hiding. I will face this.

This is wisdom: knowing when to prepare and when to act. Knowing when to bend and when to stand firm. Knowing when to send others forward and when to go forward yourself.

Reflection and Growth

This week, as we read Parshas Vayishlach, we're invited to consider our own lives through this lens:

On Preparation:

● What situations in my life require more information before I act? Am I sending out "scouts" to understand the reality I'm facing?

● Have I been preparing myself spiritually and physically for the challenges I know are coming?

● Is there something I've been avoiding because I don't feel ready? What would it take for me to feel ready?

On Standing in Front:

● What do I hold most precious and dear? My family, my values, my beliefs, my community?

● Am I willing to stand in front to protect these things, or do I hide behind others?

● When was the last time I took a stand for something that mattered, even when it was difficult or risky?

On Growth:

● What middos do I need to refine to be the kind of leader who can stand in front when needed?

● How are my spiritual practices affecting my physical life? How is my physical discipline affecting my spiritual growth?

● Am I in a cycle of growth, where body and soul elevate each other, or am I stuck?

Closing Thought

Yaakov teaches us that true leadership isn't about being the strongest or the loudest. It's about knowing when to gather information and when to act. It's about standing in front when it matters most, protecting what we hold dear by placing ourselves at risk.

It's about the courage to face our fears, to wrestle with our challenges, and to emerge transformed, ready to stand at the head.

May we all merit to know when to prepare and when to act, when to send others forward and when to go forward ourselves. May we have the wisdom to distinguish between harm that builds and danger that destroys. And may we always have the courage to stand in front when it truly matters.

Have a wonderful Shabbos.

Parashat Vayeishev: Settling and Motion — The Journey Toward Responsibility

A personal note: this dvar Torah was prepared in the middle of a move. Life happens. But that is never an excuse to let go of Torah — we always have to keep it close, dear to our hearts, in our minds, and in our words.

Settling — and Then the Storm

The parsha opens with the word vayeishev — and he settled. There is a connotation of rest, of a fixed place, of a person finding their footing. Yaakov, after all his years of struggle with Lavan, after the confrontation with Eisav, after the loss of Rachel — he seeks to settle. To breathe.

But the Torah doesn't let him. Almost immediately, everything breaks open. The sale of Yosef. The incident of Yehuda and Tamar. This is a parsha of enormous motion, even as it begins with stillness. And perhaps that is the lesson embedded in the very first word: when we seek to settle too comfortably, Hashem often has other plans.

Yosef and His Brothers: A Complicated Truth

The sale of Yosef is one of the most emotionally charged episodes in the entire Torah. How could the Shevatim — tzaddikim — do such a thing?

The commentaries wrestle with this deeply. On one hand, Yosef was known to speak critically of his brothers, to bring dibah ra'ah — negative reports — to their father (Bereishis 37:2). He was, in certain ways, a tattle-tale, and his brothers had real grievances. His dreams, too — that they would all bow to him — were not delivered with the refined humility he had yet to develop. He had not yet learned the lesson Yaakov had mastered: the beauty and balance of tiferet, speaking both inward and outward with wisdom and care.

On the other hand, his brothers' response was extreme. And yet — Yosef himself, much later, would tell them: Ani Yosef — I am Yosef. Do not be distressed. Hashem sent me before you to preserve life (Bereishis 45:5). You were His agents. Everything unfolded as part of His plan.

This is a profound teaching. We don't always understand why things happen to us — why we are thrown into pits, why relationships break down, why we are sent somewhere we never asked to go. But the tov is always there, even when buried deeply. Hashem's plan moves forward even through human failing.

Yehuda and Tamar: When We Fall

The episode of Yehuda and Tamar arrives as an apparent digression — right in the middle of the Yosef narrative. But it belongs here.

Yehuda had separated himself from his brothers (Bereishis 38:1). He was not actively maintaining those close family ties at this point in his life. And when a person disconnects from their relationships — from family, from community, from the values that anchor them — they become vulnerable. Yehuda found himself in a compromised moment, with someone he didn't recognize, acting in a way that did not reflect his highest self.

Contrast this with Yosef. Yosef, too, was far from home. He hadn't spoken with his father in years. He was a slave in a foreign land. And yet, when Potifar's wife tempted him, he resisted. The commentaries explain that at that moment, he saw the demut deyokno shel aviv — the image of his father's face — before him (Sotah 36b). The relationship, the values, the closeness he had maintained with Yaakov — even across years and distance — gave him the koach to say no.

Connection to family, to mentors, to those who shaped us — these are not just emotional comforts. They are spiritual anchors. They hold us steady when the currents are strong.

Falling and Rising: The Twofold Message

Both Yosef and Yehuda stumbled in different ways. Yosef's words and his gaavah — his pride — created the friction that led to his being sold. Yehuda gave in to a moment of passion. Both are human. Both reflect the natural tendencies we all carry.

But here is the crucial difference: neither stayed down.

Yehuda, once he realized the truth — that it was Tamar, his own daughter-in-law, who had acted out of a legitimate claim — immediately declared tzadkah mimeni, she is more righteous than I (Bereishis 38:26). He owned it. Publicly. Immediately. No deflection, no excuse. That moment of kabbalas achrayus — accepting responsibility — was transformative. From this union, the dynasty of Malkhut Yisrael would eventually emerge. From this low point, the line of David and Mashiach begins.

The Torah is teaching us: we are not supposed to give in to ra, to ta'avah. But if we do stumble, we must not let the failure define us permanently. There is kedushah to accomplish even from the lowest places. Hashem sends us these tests — these curveballs, as life calls them — for a reason. There is both a lesson and a mission within each one.

Closing Reflection

Vayeishev is a parsha about the gap between where we think we are and where Hashem is taking us. Yaakov wanted to settle. Yosef thought his destiny was one thing and found himself in a pit. Yehuda wandered and fell. And yet — from all of it — the foundations of the Jewish future were being laid.

We are all in the middle of something. A move, a struggle, a moment of uncertainty. The Torah asks us not to wait until we are settled to hold it close. Keep it in your heart and your mouth, especially when life is in motion. That is precisely when it matters most.

Gut Shabbos.

Reflection Questions

Where in my life am I holding a grievance that might be obscuring a larger divine purpose?

Who are the people whose demut — whose image and values — keeps me grounded when I am far from home or far from myself?

Is there a place where I have stumbled and stayed down too long? What would it look like to own it fully, like Yehuda, and move forward?

How do I hold both the reality of human failing and the truth of Hashem's plan at the same time, without using one to excuse the other?

Parashat Mikeitz: Light from Within — Yosef, Chanukah, and the Courage to Remain Ourselves

What a powerful convergence this Shabbos brings: Erev Shabbos Mikeitz, Chanukah, and Rosh Chodesh — all arriving together. In fact, this is the Shabbos of the longest Birkat Hamazon of the year, because we have all the additions at once: Ya'aleh v'Yavo, Al HaNissim, and Retzeh. A rare and beautiful stacking of holiness.

But let us not just celebrate the confluence. Let us find the message that runs through all of it.

Yosef's Teshuvah: Learning Humility the Hard Way

When we left off in Vayeishev, Yosef was in prison. And here in Mikeitz, the time finally comes for him to be released — but not before an important reckoning. The commentaries teach that Yosef's imprisonment was extended by two additional years precisely because he had asked the Sar HaMashkim, the royal cupbearer, to remember him and advocate on his behalf to Paroh (Bereishis 40:14). He requested human intervention rather than placing his full trust in Hashem.

Now, this is not to say that hishtadlus — making an effort — is wrong. But Yosef, at that particular level of his spiritual growth, was being called to something higher: pure bitachon. To do his job, to remain who he was, and to trust that Hashem would take care of the rest. That small reliance on mortal intervention — even well-intentioned — came with a cost.

And we need to understand why this cost existed. This wasn't Yosef's first lesson in humility. Remember how he ended up in that pit to begin with. He was known for his dreams — dreams in which his brothers and even his parents bowed to him. He was known to speak critically of his brothers. He was called ba'al hachalamot, the dreamer. There was truth in his visions. But the way he delivered the message was not yet refined enough. He was still learning how to carry greatness without letting it overflow into arrogance.

So here we are, years later, with the added two years of imprisonment, and the lesson has finally landed.

Standing Before Paroh: A New Yosef

When Yosef is finally brought before Paroh, notice how the scene is framed. The Torah describes him being rushed from the pit — vayeritsuhu min habor — and he changes his clothes and stands before the most powerful man in the world. He is introduced as a na'ar Ivri, a young Hebrew man, a prisoner. In that era and context, being identified as a Jew, a Hebrew, was not a badge of honor in the palace of Mitzrayim.

And yet — the Midrash teaches something remarkable. As Yosef ascended the steps toward Paroh's throne, he spoke with him in every language imaginable. And then he whispered one more language into Paroh's ear — a language Paroh did not know. According to the Midrash, the law of Mitzrayim held that whoever knew the most languages was qualified to rule. By whispering that final language, Yosef was not showing off. He was doing something far more sophisticated: he was quietly demonstrating his qualifications without embarrassing Paroh, without proclaiming "I should be king," without making anyone feel small. He shared the insight privately, humbly, between the two of them.

This is the new Yosef. He has learned anavah, true humility. Not the false humility of hiding one's gifts, but the refined humility of knowing how and when and to whom to present them. His message was true. His capability was real. But now it was delivered with shiflus, with grace, without arrogance.

When Paroh then asks him to interpret the dreams, Yosef says immediately: Biladai — it is not me. Elokim ya'aneh et shalom Paroh — Hashem will provide Paroh's answer (Bereishis 41:16). Not "I am a gifted interpreter." Not "Hashem gave this to me and I'll explain it." Just: this is Hashem's word, and here it is. The focus moves entirely off himself.

The Rambam and True Teshuvah

The Rambam teaches that the ultimate test of teshuvah is facing the same situation again and choosing differently (Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1). Real change is not declared — it is demonstrated. Yosef had done teshuvah. We can see it in how he stands before Paroh: the same stage, the same pressure, the same opportunity to elevate himself — and this time, he channels it all toward Hashem. Biladi — not me.

And the test for his brothers is structured the same way. Yosef tests them throughout this parsha: Are they the same people who threw him into a pit? When BinYamin is threatened, will they abandon him as they once abandoned Yosef? We see the answer unfolding — the full resolution comes next week in Vayigash — but the test is rooted in this exact principle. Can they face the same situation and choose differently?

Rosh Chodesh and the Jewish Calendar: Masters of Time

There's another dimension to this Shabbos: Rosh Chodesh. And it connects to something deeper about Jewish identity.

This week, I was in the office speaking with a colleague — a wonderful person, raised Jewish in Turkey. We were talking about birthdays and calendar dates. When she asked me when my "real" birthday was and I gave her the Hebrew date, she was surprised. She had grown up with the sense that the Jewish calendar was secondary — the "other" calendar, not the real one.

I corrected her gently. The Jewish calendar is my real calendar. If you want to know the date the rest of the world uses, I can tell you that too — but that's the secondary one, not the primary. She smiled, and we had a beautiful conversation about what that means.

But the exchange stuck with me. Because this is exactly the issue of Chanukah.

The Real Message of Chanukah

People often reduce Chanukah to a comfortable message: "be yourself, don't let anyone erase your identity, we can all get along." And while there is truth in that, it misses the sharper edge of the holiday. The Yevanim — the Greeks — were not asking the Jews to disappear. They were asking the Jews to integrate. To modernize. To let go of the particularities and join the broader, enlightened civilization. To stop being different.

And the Chashmonaim said: No.

Not "no, we can't coexist." But: "No, we will not give up who we are, even if it makes us uncomfortable, even if it makes us stand out, even if it feels easier to blend in." The Jewish people are supposed to be ohr lagoyim — a light unto the nations. But a ray of light only illuminates the world because it comes from outside. A ray that is absorbed into the wall doesn't light the room. We have to remain separate in order to shine.

This week, there was a terrible incident in Australia — an antisemitic attack that left our community shaken. A friend asked me: will the Chabad shluchim continue their public Chanukah events? Will they keep lighting the menorah in public spaces when it feels so dangerous?

I said: more than ever they will have to. Because the message of Chanukah is the answer to that question. Our neshamah is godly. Hashem placed us in this physical world to be a representation of that godliness. If we retreat from who we are under pressure, we are not keeping ourselves safe — we are losing ourselves. History has shown, again and again, that conformity does not protect us. The people who were targeted were often those who had already given the most ground.

Yosef understood this. When he stood before Paroh — the most powerful man in the world, surrounded by star-readers and sorcerers who had all failed — Yosef did not say "look at me, a clever Jew." He said: Elokim will answer. He showed the world not himself, but the One behind him. That is what it means to be a light. Not "look how great I am." But "look how great is the Source from which I shine."

Closing Reflection

As we light the Chanukah candles this Shabbos — with Rosh Chodesh adding its own layer of kedushah, with Mikeitz reminding us of Yosef's transformation — we are invited to ask ourselves: Have I done my own teshuvah? Have I learned to carry my gifts with humility? And am I willing to remain who I am, even when the world is asking me to be someone else?

The lights we kindle face outward. That is halacha — ner Chanukah mitzvah lehanicha al petach beito mibachutz, we place them where the world can see. But the light itself must come from within. From our neshamah. From our connection to Hashem. That connection is what makes us a light. Not conformity. Not blending in. Us — fully, unapologetically, humbly us.

Gut Shabbos. Freilichen Chanukah. Chodesh Tov.

Reflection Questions

Where in my life have I been relying too heavily on human intervention, rather than trusting Hashem while doing my hishtadlus?

Have I truly done teshuvah in an area that matters — and have I been tested in the same situation again? How did I respond?

Am I willing to be visibly, proudly Jewish even when it feels uncomfortable or dangerous? What does that look like practically in my life?

How can I shine outward without losing the inner source of that light?
